pedagogy.summary: Two fractions are equivalent when they mark the SAME point / the same magnitude on the number line (or the same length on a strip), even though they are written with different numerators and denominators. Families such as 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 arise because re-partitioning each unit part into finer equal parts leaves the position unchanged. Stacked and aligned number lines, and dual labels above/below one line, make the coincident points visible.
bestPractices: Use stacked 0–1 number lines (halves, thirds, fourths … tenths — IES Figure 4) and read off the points that line up.
Label one set of fractions above a single line and another set below it, pointing to 1/2 and 4/8 at the same spot (IES fix for Roadblock 2.3).
Measure equal lengths with different fraction strips (IES Figure 5) to feel 'same size'.
Practise the documented hard case: find an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line (e.g. 1/2 on a line divided into sixths).
Insist that 'same point = same number', directly countering the belief that different symbols must mean different amounts.
keyRepresentations: One line with dual labels above and below (1/2 above, 4/8 below at one point)
Fraction strips of different unit sizes compared by length
commonMisconceptions: Cannot accept two differently-written fractions as the same point (IES Roadblock 2.3)
Cannot locate an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line (e.g. finding 1/2 as 3/6 on a sixths line)
'Different numbers can't name the same amount' — denies equivalence altogether
Additive drift — thinks 1/2 and 2/3 are equivalent because you 'add 1 to each'
Whole-number bias — 2/4 must be bigger than 1/2 because the numbers are larger

learn.summary: Two fractions are equivalent when they mark the SAME point (same magnitude) on a number line or the same length on a strip, even though they are written with different numerators and denominators. Families such as 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 arise because re-partitioning each unit part into finer equal parts leaves the position unchanged. Stacked/aligned 0–1 number lines, dual labels above and below one line, and length-matched fraction strips make the coincident points visible. The documented hard cases are (a) accepting two differently-written fractions as the same point and (b) finding an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line (e.g. locating 1/2 as 3/6 on a line divided into sixths). Re-partitioning only produces a new name when the finer parts subdivide evenly all the way to the point.

activities.title: Plumb-line on stacked thirds and sixths lines
feedback: If a learner reads off 4/6 for the point under 2/3, confirm the shared point and ask them to measure both lengths from 0 to check they match.
If a learner insists 2/3 and 4/6 differ because the numbers differ, dual-label the single point (2/3 above, 4/6 below) and measure both lengths from 0 to show they coincide.
Probe: 'How many sixths make one half? Show me the jumps on the line.' (Answer: three sixths reach the midpoint, so 3/6 = 1/2.)
activities.rationale: Aligning lines and reading off coincident points directly addresses the documented difficulty of accepting two equivalent fractions as the same point. A live plumb-line and dual labels make the mechanism concrete; a static stacked diagram can serve the same role but cannot be re-aligned by the learner. Efficacy over other media is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Equivalent fractions are those representing the same numerical value; number lines and stacked/dual-labelled lines are the recommended tools, and students find it hard to see two equivalent fractions as the same point (Roadblock 2.3) or to find an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line. Recommendation 2 is rated moderate evidence.
learnerActions: Stack a 0–1 line divided into thirds directly above a 0–1 line divided into sixths, carefully aligned at 0 and 1.
Point to 2/3 on the thirds line and drop a vertical plumb-line straight down to the sixths line.
Name the fraction on the sixths line that sits at exactly the same point (4/6), and state in words: two different names, one position.
Repeat for other target points and record each equivalent pair you find.
Say aloud why the shared point means the two fractions are equal in size.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent fractions are different names for the SAME point on the number line; same position means same magnitude.

activities.title: Re-partition toggle: the point that does not move
feedback: Ask: 'When you split each third into two to make sixths, did the 2/3 mark move? Why not?' (It stays put; subdividing parts does not change position.)
If a learner claims 'there is no 1/2 on the sixths line', have them split each half into three and count the three sixths to the midpoint, then mark 3/6 on the 1/2 point.

Ask: 'Is there a fraction written in fifths that equals 1/2? Why or why not?' Use this to surface that 1/2 cannot be written as a whole number of fifths (1/2 = 2.5/5), so no fifths mark lands on it — re-partitioning only renames a point when the parts divide evenly to reach it.
activities.rationale: Explicitly re-partitioning while watching the mark stay put addresses the crux difficulty of finding an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line, and explains WHY families arise rather than just listing them. Live subdivision makes the invariance visible; a prepared sequence of printed lines can approximate it.
sourceClaims: Equivalent fractions are those representing the same numerical value; number lines and stacked/dual-labelled lines are the recommended tools, and students find it hard to see two equivalent fractions as the same point (Roadblock 2.3) or to find an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line. Recommendation 2 is rated moderate evidence.
learnerActions: Start on a thirds line with 2/3 marked.
Split each third into two equal parts to create a sixths line, keeping the 0–1 ends fixed.
Observe whether the 2/3 mark moves, and add the new label 4/6 to that same point.
Explain in your own words why subdividing each part does not shift the position, only adds a finer-grained name.
Now locate 1/2 on a line divided into sixths by splitting each half into three (not two): count three sixths to the midpoint and mark 3/6 at the 1/2 point.
activities.intendedInsight: Re-partitioning each unit part into finer equal parts preserves a fraction's position, which is why equivalent families exist. When the finer partition subdivides evenly all the way to the point, that same point simply gains a new name (1/2 becomes 3/6 on a sixths line); when the partition does not reach the point (e.g. fifths for 1/2), no such name exists.

activities.title: Measuring equal lengths with different fraction strips
feedback: If a learner lists 2/4 and 3/6 but cannot explain why, link back to the re-partition reasoning: each half splits evenly into the finer parts, so the endpoint does not move.
Ask the learner to produce one fraction that is NOT equal to 1/2 but lands near it, and one that IS equal to it, then justify each on the strip or line.
activities.rationale: A length model gives a second sense of 'same size' that complements the point model and supports generating a full equivalent family, meeting the curriculum expectation to show families of equivalents using diagrams. Physical strips and card cutouts are approximations to the idealised zero-thickness lengths they represent.
sourceClaims: Pupils recognise and show, using diagrams, families of common equivalent fractions in KS2 (Years 3–4).
learnerActions: Lay a 1/2 strip, a 2/4 strip and a 3/6 strip along the same 0–1 length.
Check by eye and by measuring that they reach the same endpoint (allowing for the slight thickness and cutting error of physical strips).
State that 'same length = same number' even though the pieces and labels differ.
Find and record at least three fractions equal to 1/2 using the strips and/or a number line (e.g. 2/4, 3/6, 5/10).
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalence can also be felt as equal length: differently-partitioned strips that reach the same point name the same amount.

activities.title: Contrast renaming with 'add one to each'
feedback: If a learner names 3/4 as equal to 2/3, place both on the shared line and show 3/4 (0.75) lies further right than 2/3 (about 0.667), then contrast the +1 shift with even subdivision.

If a learner says 2/4 must be bigger than 1/2 'because the numbers are larger', return to the shared point/length to show the two coincide; larger numerator and denominator here do not mean a larger amount.
activities.rationale: Juxtaposing additive drift and whole-number-bias errors against the same-point model lets learners see why these shortcuts fail on the line, rather than only being told they are wrong.
sourceClaims: Equivalent fractions are those representing the same numerical value; number lines and stacked/dual-labelled lines are the recommended tools, and students find it hard to see two equivalent fractions as the same point (Roadblock 2.3) or to find an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line. Recommendation 2 is rated moderate evidence.
learnerActions: On a shared 0–1 line with 2/3 marked, predict where 3/4 (from 'add 1 to top and bottom') would land.
Place 3/4 on the line and observe it sits to the RIGHT of 2/3, at a different point.
Compare this +1 shift with splitting each part into finer pieces, which did not move the mark.
Explain why adding the same number to numerator and denominator is NOT the same as finding an equivalent.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalence is a shared point produced by re-partitioning; adding the same amount to numerator and denominator is not a valid way to find equivalents, because for any fraction other than one whole it moves the point (2/3 -> 3/4 is further right), so the new fraction is not equivalent. (The only exception is a fraction equal to 1, such as 2/2 -> 3/3, which stays at 1.)

activities.title: Verify and sort equivalents (practice and check)
feedback: For each decision, require the learner to point to the position or length that justifies it, not just a symbolic rule.
If a sorting error appears, return to the shared line to locate both fractions before correcting.
activities.rationale: Verification and sorting consolidate and check the concept after it has been constructed and apply the same-value definition directly (e.g. 'do 2/3 and 4/6 land on the same point?'); this is practice/assessment support, so it should follow, not replace, the construction activities above. A sort can check classification but does not itself elicit the physical re-partitioning or the explanation of why the point does not move.
sourceClaims: Equivalent fractions are those representing the same numerical value; number lines and stacked/dual-labelled lines are the recommended tools, and students find it hard to see two equivalent fractions as the same point (Roadblock 2.3) or to find an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line. Recommendation 2 is rated moderate evidence.
learnerActions: Decide for pairs such as 'do 2/3 and 4/6 land on the same point?' and justify using a line or strip.
Match equivalent fractions to a target fraction.
Sequence a set of fractions in order along a number line.
Sort cards into 'equivalent to 1/2' and 'not equivalent to 1/2', explaining each placement.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the same-point idea is built, learners can reliably verify, match and sort equivalents and justify their decisions by position or length.

constraints: Target understanding (REPRESENTATIONAL): learners should locate, generate and explain equivalents, not just recognise them.

A fraction wall or stacked-line reference that only highlights a family (e.g. tap 1/2 -> highlights 2/4, 3/6, 4/8) is a useful recall/reference scaffold but does not let the learner re-partition, so it cannot by itself build the crux differently-partitioned case; use it alongside, not instead of, re-partitioning work.

Verification/matching/sorting tasks consolidate and assess classification but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a family or an explanation of why the point does not move; pair them with construction activities.

Full understanding requires generating a correct family for 1/2 AND explaining equivalence as re-partitioning that preserves position AND correctly rejecting a non-equivalent (e.g. recognising that no fraction written in fifths equals 1/2, since no fifths mark lands on it). Reading off a single aligned equivalent is only partial.
Fraction strips and card cutouts have slight physical thickness; treat them as approximations to the ideal zero-thickness lengths and points on an idealised number line.

Re-partitioning only yields an equivalent when each unit part subdivides evenly to the point: 1/2 can be named in sixths (3/6, each half split into three) but cannot be written as any whole number of fifths, so no fifths mark lands on 1/2. Keep this condition explicit — never describe a half as simply 'absent from the line'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed 3D 'adds nothing' and that dialogue/conversation could not teach this because equivalence 'is planar' and 'built by aligning and re-partitioning, not by in-role dialogue'. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established comparative-efficacy findings, and have been softened/omitted: a number-line/length focus is well justified here, but universal necessity or medium-superiority claims are not asserted.
The IES claim is marked verified in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:false. Treat the curriculum citation as an expectation statement, not as efficacy evidence.

Arithmetic checked: 1/2 = 2.5/5 is not a fifths gridpoint, so no fifths-partition mark equals 1/2; applying +1 to top and bottom of 2/3 gives 3/4 = 0.75 > 2/3 (about 0.667), correctly further right; 2/4, 3/6 and 5/10 all equal 1/2; three sixths reach the midpoint (3/6 = 1/2); halves become sixths by splitting each half into three, thirds become sixths by splitting each third into two.

Editorial correction (no new source check): the original row's 'full' level and discriminator phrased the fifths non-example as '1/2 is not a point on a fifths line'. This was tightened to 'no fraction written in fifths equals 1/2 / no fifths mark lands on it', since 1/2 is a magnitude present on any 0–1 line and only its fifths-partition naming is impossible.

probeDeeper: When you split each third into two to make sixths, did the 2/3 mark move? Why not?
Is 1/2 on a line divided into fifths? Why or why not?
Give me a fraction that is NOT equal to 1/2 but lands near it, and one that IS equal to it.
How many sixths make one half? Show me the jumps on the line.
assess.correctAnswer: 4/6 is at the same point as 2/3 — same position means same magnitude, so 2/3 = 4/6 (each third splits into two sixths, the point does not move). Three fractions equal to 1/2: e.g. 2/4, 3/6, 5/10, each marking the midpoint of 0–1.

errorPatterns.pattern: Same-point denied — 'the dots are in the same place but the numbers are different, so they can't be equal'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Dual-label the single point (2/3 above, 4/6 below) and measure both lengths from 0 to show they match
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses to accept 2/3 = 4/6 despite the shared point

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive equivalence — offers 3/4 (or treats 1/2 ≈ 2/3) as equal by 'adding 1 to top and bottom'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place both on the shared line; show 3/4 sits to the right of 2/3; contrast the +1 shift with splitting each part
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names 3/4 as equal to 2/3, or places supposed equivalents at different points

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot find an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line — 'there is no 1/2 on the sixths line'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count sixths to the midpoint (three of them) and mark 3/6 on the 1/2 point
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Locates 1/2 among halves but says it is absent from a sixths line

responseLevels.gap: Treats differently-written fractions as necessarily different amounts; cannot find an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line.
responseLevels.full: Identifies same-point equivalence, generates a correct family for 1/2, explains equivalence as re-partitioning that preserves position, and correctly rejects a non-equivalent (e.g. 1/2 is not a point on a fifths line).
responseLevels.partial: Reads off an aligned equivalent (4/6 = 2/3) from stacked lines but cannot generate a family independently or explain why the point does not move — lists 2/4, 3/6 without the re-partition reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show stacked 0-to-1 number lines, one divided into thirds and one into sixths, lined up. Point to 2/3 on the thirds line and ask: 'Which fraction on the sixths line is at exactly the same point, and how do you know they are equal?' Then ask: 'Show me on these lines three fractions that are all equal to 1/2.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads equivalence as same-point identifies 4/6 and generates a correct family. The Roadblock-2.3 child insists 2/3 and 4/6 differ because the numbers differ; the additive child offers 3/4 ('2/3 plus one to each'); the whole-number-bias child says 4/6 is bigger. Both moves — interpret the aligned point and produce a family — are required.

Recommendation 2 is rated moderate evidence.
